Question: Why do some people choose not to spay or neuter their pets? What are some of the arguments they give and what are the benefits of spaying or neutering animals?
Answer: So, Eddie went to the vet today. I've been considering neutering him, because all the rabbit websites and YouTubers say it's imperative, and I wanted a full exam done. (My vet is a rabbit specialist recommended by the House Rabbit Society, among other rabbit organizations, for the record.) Well, after the exam, the doc told me that he seems to be in excellent health, and that as long as he's happy, healthy, and not showing the negative behaviors associated with not being neutered — which in male rabbits usually means aggression, humping everything in their general vicinity, and spraying urine all over the place — that it's not worth the risk of the surgery and anesthesia. (She did also stress that if he was a female, she would insist on spaying, because unspayed female rabbits are at risk of serious health conditions, especially uterine or ovarian cancer, as they age. Unaltered male rabbits are not subject to the same health risks, as testicular/prostate cancer is extremely rare in rabbits.) I told her I know he can't ever have a rabbit companion unless he gets neutered (although I am not in a position to be able to get a second rabbit at present), and she said some rabbits can be fine without another rabbit, that bonding often fails, and as long as he doesn't seem to be lonely or depressed, he's probably okay being alone provided he gets enough attention and love (and I assure you, he does). Because he is still young, I can also opt to neuter him later if I decide to get another rabbit. I'll be honest — I was incredibly relieved to hear her say this. Eddie is my whole world, and if I put him through an elective surgery and something went wrong, I would end up in a padded room. I've read so many horror stories of male rabbits who are holy terrors due to hormones — biting, lunging, charging, humping everyone and everything, spraying urine on everyone and everything, etc. That just isn't Eddie. He's a super mellow, ridiculously sweet little guy, and the worst of his hormonal behavior (which invariably comes in spring) amounts to him circling my feet, and pooping and maybe dribbling a little pee on the couch here and there for a month or so (my couch is covered by a waterproof couch protector). Then he's back to not peeing or pooping anywhere but in his litterbox, and even when he's hormonal, he's as sweet as ever. (I even got him a stuffed animal, figuring he could vent his sexual frustration by humping it, but he never has. He mostly just ignores it.) So for me, the reason I am not currently planning on neutering my rabbit is that the potential benefits of doing so do not outweigh the inherent risks that come with surgery. Rabbits are delicate creatures, and putting them under anesthesia carries more risk than it does with a dog or cat. If he is happy, and my very qualified and experienced rabbit vet advises against neutering him at this time, I see no reason to do it.

Question: Can you become a great Hollywood movie star without being particularly beautiful?
Answer: Sure. Of course the first person who came to mind was the great Kathy Bates. She's not an ugly woman, but perhaps best described as “plain", and she became a star as a middle-aged, overweight woman at a time when the term “body positivity” didn't exist in Hollywood. Judy Garland wasn't a great beauty, either. That's partly why her life became so tragic, because she spent so much time trying to be that great beauty. Perhaps one of my all-time favorite character actors was the legendary Anne Revere, who was among the most sought-after actresses of the 1940s and landed an Oscar, along with two other nominations, before being blacklisted in 1950 for refusing to testify before the House Un-American Activities Committee during the Red Scare. The most one could say about Anne's appearance would be to call her “handsome” — she was never beautiful. I'll also mention Frances McDormand, who was absolutely a beautiful woman in her younger years, but has aged naturally, with no fillers, facelifts, hair dye, teeth whiteners, etc., and has had probably her greatest success as an actor in her 60s. How many female actors pick up their Oscars with messy hair and not a smidge of makeup on their faces? Lastly, there's THE great Hollywood movie star, Meryl Streep. I think Meryl is stunning, but she is and was not a conventional beauty, and in fact she was rejected many times early in her career for not being beautiful enough, most famously by Dino DiLaurentiis when she auditioned for the female lead in the 1976 remake of King Kong. DiLaurentiis basically called her “it", as well as “so ugly". Didn't stop her from becoming probably the most acclaimed American actor of all time. I'll also note, Hollywood beauty also has its share of smoke and mirrors. The average person walking down the street doesn't have a team of hairstylists, makeup artists, waxers, manicurists, nutritionists, personal trainers, etc. to keep them looking glamorous. If you look at Jennifer Lopez back when she was a Fly Girl on In Living Color, she was obviously attractive, but nowhere near as sleek and glamorous as we know her now. Just a cute girl from the Bronx. And if you were to see J. Lo even now when she wakes up in the morning, you might not recognize her.

Question: Should I surrender my guinea pig if the other died and is sad? I got them when I was younger and now that I am older I just don’t have time for it anymore.
Answer: If your pig is lonely and you aren't interested in having it anymore (because let's be honest, when someone says they “don't have time” for an animal anymore, that's usually what they mean), then yes, you should absolutely find a rescue or shelter near you that takes guinea pigs. No reason to condemn the poor animal to a lonely life of neglect, even if he or she is older. Please do not just give the pig away for free to some random stranger — there are a lot of sickos out there who will harm animals, he could be tortured, fed to a snake, etc. If you decide to rehome your pig yourself rather than surrendering him to a rescue or shelter, charge a rehoming or adoption fee of at least $30 USD and vet anyone who shows interest, to make sure he goes to a good home. While I appreciate you thinking of the pig's happiness, the question illustrates a very common occurrence, and why I don't think kids should have pets, aside from family pets like a dog or cat. A guinea pig's lifespan is about five to seven years on average. That's something you should know before you get guinea pigs, and it needs to be considered where you're going to be in 5 or 6 years. While a pig's lifespan is longer than that of most rodent pets, 7 years is just not that long, and yet you suddenly “don't have time" for your pig anymore, because you were younger when you got guinea pigs, and now you're older and you have more important things to do. So this animal that I assume you've had for at least several years is now unwanted and going to be tossed out like an old toy that you've outgrown. Please, people, I'm begging you: do not get your kids pets that are their pets. If it's not going to belong to the entire family, don't do it. The vast majority of the time, this is the end result. They're not toys, they're living beings.

Question: Why don't famous authors collaborate on books? Why haven't JK Rowling and Rick Riordan co-written a book? Wouldn't it become very popular?
Answer: Stephen King and Peter Straub — two giants of American horror fiction — became friends after meeting in London in 1977 and discovering that each was a fan of the other's work. They would subsequently collaborate on The Talisman. It spent 12 weeks at #1 on the New York Times Bestseller List when it was released in 1984. Indeed, it was popular enough with fans that seventeen years later, King and Straub decided to write a sequel, which was critically lauded and also a #1 bestseller. Authors will collaborate with one another, but it's not going to happen willy-nilly — like, “oh, you're popular, I'm popular, let's write a book together!” They have to have something to work with other than both simply being popular. Otherwise it's just a gimmick.

Question: Who was the very first teen idol?
Answer: The general consensus is that the first artist who could be considered a teen idol was Hungarian composer Franz Liszt (1811–1886). Liszt was a handsome and reportedly magnetic young man, and young women responded accordingly even in the 1840s. There was even a term coined for the phenomenon: “Lisztomania". Women would try to snip locks of his hair, steal his handkerchiefs and piano strings, and one reportedly even snatched up a used cigar butt he had tossed away, which she then enclosed in a locket with his initials on it. Liszt in 1858: The first teen idol in the modern sense may have been Frank Sinatra (1915–1998). Like Liszt, the legions of screaming teenage girls who descended upon his concerts in the early 1940s led a term to be coined, this time “Sinatramania”. He was given nicknames like “Swoonatra”, and his young fans took to calling themselves “Sinatratics". Young women regularly accosted him trying to steal his clothing right off his person, and would bribe hotel maids to let them touch his bed. Ol' Blue Eyes certainly had it going on in the 1940s.
